source_read: PMC HTML full text PMC4827335, the NIH author manuscript (NIHMS762992) of N Engl J Med 2014;370(23):2219-2227, read in full in my own browser tab in one untruncated text extraction: unheaded introduction, all ADVERSE EFFECTS subsections, LIMITATIONS OF THE EVIDENCE AND GAPS IN KNOWLEDGE with the box on medical uses, CONCLUSIONS, Tables 1 and 2 with footnotes, the legends of Figures 1 and 2, footnotes, all 77 references and the author-information panel. The images of Figures 1 and 2 were not viewed; the NEJM disclosure forms were not read.

claims.overstatement: None. 'Links repeated use with increased vomiting without a citation' matches the source, which says only that hyperemesis has been reported with repeated use.
claims.note: The sentence carries no reference number; the review gives no frequency, features or course of the syndrome.

anchors.locator: LIMITATIONS OF THE EVIDENCE AND GAPS IN KNOWLEDGE › box (Clinical Conditions with Symptoms That May Be Relieved by Treatment with Marijuana or Other Cannabinoids) › Nausea
anchors.extracted: After describing THC as an antiemetic, the box adds that increased vomiting (hyperemesis) has paradoxically been reported with repeated marijuana use; no citation, frequency or description of the syndrome is given.

claims.overstatement: None as to Volkow. The review's own language is causal (the evidence 'clearly indicates' that long-term use can lead to addiction; Table 1 lists addiction as an effect of long-term or heavy use), and the claim rightly keeps to association.
claims.note: All Volkow figures re-found. Precision point: in Volkow the 9% is cited to Lopez-Quintero et al. 2011 (ref 3), while one in six and 25-50% are cited to Hall & Degenhardt 2009 (ref 4); the claim's parenthesis 'Volkow et al., 2014, citing Hall & Degenhardt, with 17% in its table' is right for one in six, but could be read as covering the 9 in 100 as well. Whether ref 4 contains the 25-50% figure cannot be judged from this source (not my source to check). No definition of daily use, no denominators and no adjustment are given with any of the figures, as the claim says. Table 1's footnote asserts, without a citation, that addiction is strongly associated with initial use early in adolescence.

anchors.locator: ADVERSE EFFECTS › RISK OF ADDICTION, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: About 9% of people who experiment with marijuana become addicted, by DSM-IV dependence criteria (ref 3, Lopez-Quintero et al. 2011); about 1 in 6 of those who start as teenagers and 25% to 50% of those who smoke daily (both cited to ref 4, Hall & Degenhardt 2009); no definitions of frequency, samples or adjustment given.

anchors.locator: ADVERSE EFFECTS › RISK OF ADDICTION, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: People who start in adolescence are about 2 to 4 times as likely as people who start in adulthood to have symptoms of cannabis dependence within 2 years of first use (ref 8, Chen, Storr & Anthony 2009); early and regular use is said to predict addiction (ref 7).

anchors.locator: Table 1 (Effects of long-term or heavy use, Addiction row) and its footnote
anchors.extracted: Addiction in about 9% of users overall, 17% of those who begin in adolescence and 25% to 50% of daily users; the footnote says the effect is strongly associated with initial use early in adolescence, with no citation.

claims.note: Volkow cites the about-9% figure to the NESARC analysis (ref 3, Lopez-Quintero et al. 2011), as the claim says, and phrases it as a lifetime projection (people who experiment 'will become addicted'), matching NESARC's cumulative probability. The same paragraph gives NSDUH 2012 counts (2.7 million with DSM-IV marijuana dependence), which the claim does not use.

anchors.locator: ADVERSE EFFECTS › RISK OF ADDICTION, 1st paragraph; Table 1 (Addiction row)
anchors.extracted: About 9% of those who experiment with marijuana will become addicted by DSM-IV dependence criteria, cited to ref 3 (Lopez-Quintero et al. 2011, NESARC); Table 1: about 9% of users overall.

claims.overstatement: None in the claim, which does not cite Volkow by name. Volkow's own wording is causal and one-sided: use is associated with vascular conditions that 'increase the risks' of heart attack, stroke and transient ischaemic attack during intoxication, with no estimates and no mention of null findings.
claims.note: Volkow is not named anywhere in the statement or magnitude; if this anchor stays, name Volkow et al. (2014) among the narrative reviews, or drop the anchor. The passage is second-hand (ref 45, a 2014 cardiology review by its title; the coronary-microcirculation statement cites refs 46 and 47, the latter a case report by its title). Table 2 does not rate cardiovascular effects.

anchors.locator: ADVERSE EFFECTS › RISK OF CANCER AND OTHER EFFECTS ON HEALTH, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Marijuana use has been associated with vascular conditions raising the risks of myocardial infarction, stroke and transient ischaemic attack during intoxication (ref 45); mechanisms are complex and not fully understood; effects on CB1 receptors in arterial vessels and on vasoactive compounds may explain effects on vascular resistance and coronary microcirculation (refs 46, 47); no figures.

claims.overstatement: None; the claim labels the statement as a narrative review's and second-hand.
claims.note: The efficacy statement cites a single 1975 trial (ref 59, Sallan et al.); the statement that patients often find marijuana more effective carries no citation. The suggestion that other compounds may enhance THC's effect cites a study in the house musk shrew (ref 60, by its title). The Limitations section also relays that the 1999 Institute of Medicine report acknowledged potential benefits for chemotherapy nausea and vomiting while urging research on synthetic or pure cannabinoids.

anchors.locator: LIMITATIONS OF THE EVIDENCE AND GAPS IN KNOWLEDGE › box (Clinical Conditions with Symptoms That May Be Relieved by Treatment with Marijuana or Other Cannabinoids) › Nausea
anchors.extracted: Chemotherapy nausea and vomiting was one of the first medical uses of THC and other cannabinoids (ref 58); THC is an effective antiemetic in chemotherapy (ref 59, Sallan et al. 1975), but patients often say marijuana suppresses nausea better (no citation); other compounds may enhance THC's effect (ref 60, an animal study by title).

anchors.locator: LIMITATIONS OF THE EVIDENCE AND GAPS IN KNOWLEDGE, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: The Institute of Medicine report (1999) acknowledges potential benefits of smoked marijuana against chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting, among other uses, and stresses research on synthetic or pharmaceutically pure cannabinoids.

claims.overstatement: Slight understatement of what the survey reported: the claim gives only the 2 of 19 families reporting freedom from seizures, while the same survey had 8 of 19 (42%) reporting a reduction of more than 80% and 6 of 19 (32%) a reduction of 25% to 60%. All are parent reports from a small self-selected survey, which the claim could say instead of giving one outcome. 'Describes only a parent survey' is right for human data; the box also cites animal evidence for cannabidiol.
claims.note: Recomputed: 2/19 = 10.5% (printed 11%), 8/19 = 42.1% (42%), 6/19 = 31.6% (32%). The statement on insufficient safety and efficacy data concerns cannabis botanicals (ref 73), not cannabidiol medicines. The animal-model citation (ref 74) is, by its title, a study of cannabidivarin-rich extracts, not of cannabidiol.

anchors.locator: LIMITATIONS OF THE EVIDENCE AND GAPS IN KNOWLEDGE › box (Clinical Conditions with Symptoms That May Be Relieved by Treatment with Marijuana or Other Cannabinoids) › Epilepsy
anchors.extracted: Small survey of parents using high-cannabidiol marijuana for their children's seizures (ref 72): of 19 families meeting inclusion criteria, 2 (11%) reported complete freedom from seizures, 8 (42%) a reduction of more than 80% and 6 (32%) a reduction of 25% to 60%; insufficient safety and efficacy data on cannabis botanicals for epilepsy (ref 73); increasing animal evidence for cannabidiol as an antiepileptic (ref 74).

claims.note: The statement concerns regular use in general and cites one cohort of young people (ref 23, Patton et al. 2002); Table 2 gives depression or anxiety medium confidence, by no stated method, which the claim need not repeat.

anchors.locator: ADVERSE EFFECTS › RELATION TO MENTAL ILLNESS, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 2
anchors.extracted: Regular use is associated with a higher risk of anxiety and depression (ref 23), but causality has not been established; other factors, and factors predisposing to both use and mental illness, make attribution to marijuana difficult; Table 2 rates depression or anxiety at medium confidence.

claims.overstatement: None in the claim, which does not cite Volkow by name. Volkow's statement that withdrawal makes cessation difficult and contributes to relapse is causal and rests on ref 5, a paper on diagnostic criteria by its title.
claims.note: Volkow is not named in the statement or magnitude; the passage supports the symptom description (irritability, sleep difficulty, dysphoria, craving, anxiety) but gives no prevalence or time course. If the anchor stays, name Volkow et al. (2014) where the symptoms are described, or drop it.

anchors.locator: ADVERSE EFFECTS › RISK OF ADDICTION, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: A bona fide cannabis withdrawal syndrome is recognized (ref 5, Gorelick et al. 2012), with irritability, sleeping difficulties, dysphoria, craving and anxiety, said to make stopping difficult and to contribute to relapse; no prevalence or time course given.

key_findings.note: Volkow part confirmed (refs 3 and 4; Table 1). The note's statement that Hall & Degenhardt (2009) lacks the daily-use figure was not checked: not my source.
The NESARC comparison in the note comes from another card and was not checked here.
Ref 17 is cited in the 3rd paragraph of EFFECT ON BRAIN DEVELOPMENT, for cannabinoid signalling in synapse formation, not for prenatal or adolescent THC effects.
Meier et al. numbers in the note come from another card; not checked here. No reference to Rogeberg (2013) or Moffitt et al. (2013) among the 77 references, confirmed.
The cross-card notes (Murray 2016, Moore 2007) not checked here.
The Asbridge and Rogeberg figures in the note not checked here.
The Callaghan figure in the note not checked here.
Add that the patient-preference statement is uncited (ref 59 sits before it).

reporting_issues.note: Confirmed that 25-50% is cited only to ref 4 and repeated in Table 1. That ref 4 lacks the figure was not checked: not my source.
Ref 37: Hartman & Huestis 2013, 'Cannabis effects on driving skills', Clin Chem.

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist, overall high. No reference among the 77 lists Volkow, Baler, Compton or Weiss (my check), so 'low' for reliance on own studies is right.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial. Verified: Table 1 and 2 framing as effects; 'results in measurable and long-lasting cognitive impairments' on ref 16; Solowij et al. (ref 31) a treatment-seeking sample by title; long-term exposure and driving cited to ref 35 only; high confidence in diminished achievement beside ref 33's shared environmental factors; hedged conclusions.

missed: Further citation mismatches, by reference title (extending RI 3): the box cites ref 60, a study in the house musk shrew, for other plant compounds enhancing THC's antiemetic effect; ref 74, a study of cannabidivarin-rich extracts, for cannabidiol's antiepileptic role in animals; refs 55 and 56 (endocannabinoids in human eye tissue; WIN55212-2) for THC, cannabinol and nabilone, but not cannabidiol, lowering intraocular pressure in rabbits; and ref 58, a review of cannabidiol, for THC's early use against chemotherapy nausea.
Box › Nausea: the statement that patients often find marijuana more effective than THC carries no citation.
RISK OF ADDICTION: that withdrawal makes stopping difficult and contributes to relapse rests on ref 5, a paper on diagnostic criteria by its title.

Funding field confirmed: the author-information panel gives all four authors at the National Institute on Drug Abuse, NIH, Bethesda; the footnotes state no potential conflict of interest; no funding statement.
